Рассчитан на 8–10 часов в неделю. После диагностики первой недели усильте слабый модуль.

## Неделя 1 — Диагностика

Полный тест по времени, включая Writing, честная проверка. Запишите ответ Part 2 на телефон и прослушайте. Переведите сырой балл Reading в band и зафиксируйте цель. Заведите словарную тетрадь по темам.

## Неделя 2 — Механика чтения

По одному типу заданий в день: True/False/Not Given, заголовки, summary completion. Сначала без таймера: точность важнее скорости. Правило недели: ответ должен подтверждаться конкретной строкой текста.

## Неделя 3 — Аудирование

Одна запись в день, затем разбор со скриптом. Диктанты на числа, даты и имена. Ежедневный shadowing 10 минут.

## Неделя 4 — Writing Task 1

По одному типу визуала в день, четыре полных ответа за неделю. Проверяйте наличие настоящего overview.

## Неделя 5 — Writing Task 2

Десять планов по пять минут, три полных эссе за 40 минут. Развивайте одну идею в абзаце, а не добавляйте новые. Сравнивайте с образцами по структуре.

## Неделя 6 — Speaking

Каждый день пять вопросов Part 1 и одна карточка Part 2 с записью. Отмечайте паузы из-за нехватки слов — это список лексики недели.

## Неделя 7 — Полные тесты

Два полных теста в условиях экзамена, в то же время суток. Разбирайте ошибки Reading по причинам: неверно понял вопрос, не знал слово, не успел, попался на Not Given.

## Неделя 8 — Закрепление

Только точечная работа: журнал ошибок, вступления Task 1, словарь, одна секция в день по таймеру. За три дня до экзамена — никакого нового материала.

## Что важнее материалов

- Журнал ошибок: ошибка, причина, правило.
- Одна статья на 800 слов в день и резюме в трёх предложениях.
- Учить слова словосочетаниями.
- С 4-й недели всё делать по таймеру.

questions.text: What does the writer find remarkable about the first migration of a young garden warbler?
choices: It reaches a destination it has never visited, without having been taught the route.
It always travels in the company of experienced adults of the same species.
It completes the journey more quickly than older birds of the same species.
It follows the coastline rather than crossing open country.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph stresses that a young warbler that has never left its birthplace still sets off in roughly the right direction and arrives in a wintering area it has never seen.

questions.text: What did the caged robins in the 1950s experiments demonstrate?
choices: Birds need a clear view of the stars in order to choose a direction.
Birds continued to prefer their migratory direction even without sight of the sky.
Birds became disoriented as soon as they were placed in circular cages.
Birds preferred the side of the cage that was best lit.
questions.explanation: The passage states that even with no view of the sky the caged birds fluttered towards the side matching their natural migratory direction.

questions.text: In what way does the avian compass differ from a hiker's compass?
choices: It works only when the bird is moving at speed.
It measures the strength of the magnetic field rather than its direction.
It responds to the angle at which field lines meet the earth rather than to polarity.
It has to be recalibrated every time the bird crosses the equator.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explains that a hiker's needle uses polarity, whereas the robin reads the inclination of the field lines.

questions.text: What conclusion is drawn from experiments in which the trigeminal nerve was temporarily blocked?
choices: The beak supplies map-like information about field intensity rather than a sense of direction.
The beak is the only organ involved in magnetic sensing.
Magnetite plays no part in navigation at all.
Birds lose the ability to migrate once the nerve is affected.
questions.explanation: Birds with a blocked trigeminal nerve still oriented correctly but could no longer judge magnetic intensity, which the passage interprets as a map rather than a compass function.

questions.text: Why does the removal of a single navigational cue rarely prevent a bird from migrating?
choices: Birds can postpone migration until conditions improve.
The magnetic sense is far stronger than all the other senses combined.
Migration routes are learned by imitation and therefore fixed.
Several navigational systems overlap and correct one another.
questions.explanation: The passage describes the magnetic sense as one instrument among several and notes that the systems overlap and correct one another.

questions.text: The robins in the 1950s cage experiments were able to see the night sky.
questions.explanation: False: the passage explicitly says the birds oriented correctly even with no view of the sky.

questions.text: Reversing the polarity of an artificial magnetic field makes a robin choose the opposite direction.
questions.explanation: False: the text states that reversing polarity leaves the bird's choice unchanged, while tilting the field confuses it.

questions.text: Cryptochrome has been identified in the retina of every migratory bird species studied so far.
questions.explanation: Not Given: the passage mentions cryptochrome in the retina but says nothing about how many species have been examined.

questions.text: Artificial lighting can pull night-flying migrants towards urban areas.
questions.explanation: True: the final paragraph states that artificial light draws nocturnal migrants off course towards cities.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: In laboratory tests, birds lose their orientation in total darkness or under ______ light alone.
questions.explanation: The cryptochrome model predicts failure in darkness or under red light, which is what laboratory tests show.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Magnetite, an ______ mineral, has been found in tissue of the upper beak.
questions.explanation: The passage describes magnetite as an iron-rich mineral located in the upper beak.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Young birds learn the rotation of the night sky by fixing on the point around which the ______ appear to turn.
questions.explanation: The paragraph on additional cues states that young birds fix on the point around which the stars appear to turn.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE OR TWO WORDS from the passage: Weak ______ noise produced by urban electrical equipment can disturb the cryptochrome compass.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph identifies weak radio-frequency noise from urban electrical equipment as a disruptive influence.

questions.text: Why did the length of an hour vary before the fourteenth century?
choices: Different regions used different counting systems.
Daylight was divided into twelve parts whatever the season.
Sundials were manufactured to inconsistent standards.
Church authorities altered the hours for religious reasons.
questions.explanation: Daylight and darkness were each divided into twelve parts, so the length of an hour changed as the amount of daylight changed.

questions.text: What advantage did the verge-and-foliot escapement have over the water clock?
choices: It required no maintenance of any kind.
It could be built much more cheaply.
It ran at the same rate at every hour and in every season.
It was small enough to be carried by an individual.
questions.explanation: The passage says the mechanism was crude but ran at the same rate in January and July, at midnight and at noon.

questions.text: Why did many of the earliest mechanical clocks have no dial?
choices: Dials were too expensive to produce at the time.
Their value lay in sounding the hours rather than displaying them.
Most of the people who used them could not read numbers.
They were installed in places where a dial would not be visible.
questions.explanation: The passage notes that early clocks were valued for striking the time rather than showing it, and many had no dial at all.

questions.text: According to the passage, what was the effect of work bells in the cloth towns?
choices: They allowed pay to be linked to measured time rather than output alone.
They shortened the working day for most weavers.
They replaced the authority of the town council.
They ended disputes between weavers and their employers.
questions.explanation: The passage states that wages could now be tied to measured time rather than to output alone, and that disputes turned on the honesty of the bell.

questions.text: What was the significance of Huygens's application of the pendulum in 1656?
choices: It made the mechanical clock cheap enough for ordinary households.
It allowed clocks to be made portable for the first time.
It removed the need for a falling weight to drive the mechanism.
It cut daily error so sharply that a minute hand became worth fitting.
questions.explanation: The passage says daily error fell from minutes to seconds and that only then did a minute hand become worth fitting.

questions.text: The identity of the inventor of the escapement is unknown.
questions.explanation: True: the passage attributes the escapement to an unknown craftsman in western Europe.

questions.text: The verge-and-foliot clock kept time more accurately than the best water clocks of its day.
questions.explanation: Not Given: the passage praises the constant rate of the escapement and calls it crude, but never compares its accuracy with that of water clocks.

questions.text: Public striking clocks were installed in northern European cities before they appeared in Italy.
questions.explanation: False: the passage says Italian and then northern cities competed to install public clocks from the 1330s.

questions.text: Historians are in agreement that the mechanical clock created the working habits of industrial society.
questions.explanation: False: the final paragraph states that historians disagree about whether the clock caused these habits or merely served them.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Water clocks were awkward instruments because they had to be ______ and ran differently as the water pressure fell.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph lists refilling, falling pressure and freezing as the drawbacks of water clocks.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: In monasteries a mechanical alarm woke the ______, who then rang the great bell for the community.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that alarms tripped a bell to rouse the sacrist, who summoned everyone else.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: A civic clock became a statement of ______ as much as a public utility.
questions.explanation: Towns competed to install public clocks, which signalled prosperity as well as serving a practical purpose.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Watches became genuinely accurate once the ______ created a commercial demand for coordinated schedules.
questions.explanation: The passage credits the railways with generating commercial demand for coordinated timekeeping.

questions.text: According to the passage, why do peatlands hold so much carbon?
choices: The plants growing on them are unusually productive.
Dead plant material decays extremely slowly rather than accumulating quickly.
They cover a far larger area than the world's forests.
They absorb carbon directly from rainwater.
questions.explanation: The passage states that peatlands achieve their carbon store not by growing quickly but by decaying slowly.

questions.text: What role does sphagnum moss play in a healthy bog?
choices: It supplies oxygen to bacteria living in the peat.
It shades the surface and lowers the temperature of the water.
It acidifies the surrounding water and retains large amounts of moisture.
It binds the peat together and prevents it from being washed away.
questions.explanation: Sphagnum is described as acidifying the water around it and holding many times its own weight in moisture, so that almost nothing rots.

questions.text: Why is the drainage of peatland so damaging?
choices: It exposes the peat to air, so carbon stored for millennia is released within decades.
It allows sphagnum moss to spread uncontrollably.
It removes the acidity that protects the surface vegetation.
It permanently prevents any plant from growing on the site.
questions.explanation: Once air reaches the peat, decomposition resumes and carbon that took thousands of years to accumulate returns to the atmosphere in decades.

questions.text: What is the first step in restoring a damaged peatland?
choices: Planting trees along the edges of the site.
Removing the upper layer of degraded peat.
Blocking the drainage channels so that water is retained.
Introducing grazing animals to control coarse vegetation.
questions.explanation: Restoration begins with blocking ditches using dams of peat, plastic piling or timber so that water is held rather than shed.

questions.text: Why may self-seeded trees be removed from a site under restoration?
choices: Their roots break up the layers of peat below the surface.
They draw water out of the ground and release it through their leaves.
They provide shelter for grazing animals.
They compete with sphagnum for nutrients in the soil.
questions.explanation: The passage notes that self-seeded trees pump water out of the ground through their leaves, which works against the aim of raising the water table.

questions.text: Peat usually builds up at a rate of roughly one millimetre a year.
questions.explanation: True: the passage gives about a millimetre a year, so a three-metre bog represents some three thousand years.

questions.text: Rewetting a bog produces an immediate improvement in its overall greenhouse gas balance.
questions.explanation: False: a rewetted bog releases methane, so for the first years the climate balance sheet can look worse rather than better.

questions.text: Cultivating sphagnum is currently more profitable than extracting peat for horticulture.
questions.explanation: Not Given: the passage says only that paludiculture crops would need to be made profitable, without comparing them with peat extraction.

questions.text: Restored peatlands can reduce the cost of treating drinking water.
questions.explanation: True: water leaving rewetted catchments carries less dissolved carbon, which lowers treatment costs.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD OR A NUMBER from the passage: Ditch blocking aims to raise the water table to within about ______ centimetres of the surface.
questions.explanation: The restoration paragraph gives a target water table within about ten centimetres of the surface.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Bare peat surfaces are often stabilised by spreading cut ______ or straw.
questions.explanation: The passage describes stabilising bare peat with cut heather or straw before reintroducing sphagnum.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Farming peatland while keeping it wet is known as ______.
questions.explanation: Paludiculture is defined in the final paragraph as keeping peatlands wet while still farming them.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: ______ are now used to measure the millimetre-scale rise and fall of bog surfaces.
questions.explanation: The passage ends by noting that satellites track the swelling and subsidence of bog surfaces as an early indicator of recovery.

questions.text: What was the central point of Herbert Simon's 1971 observation?
choices: Information will always be more valuable than the means of distributing it.
Abundant information makes human attention the scarce and valuable resource.
Advertising is the only sustainable way to fund information services.
People remember less when they are given more to read.
questions.explanation: Simon argued that information consumes attention, so where information is abundant the valuable thing becomes the capacity to attend to it.

questions.text: How do most large online platforms generate revenue?
choices: By charging users a subscription for access.
By selling data directly to government agencies.
By selling advertising, so income rises with the engagement they capture.
By taking a commission on goods sold through their services.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that platforms are free to use and earn revenue from advertising, so income rises with time and engagement captured.

questions.text: How is collaborative filtering described in the passage?
choices: It recommends to a user the items chosen by similar users.
It ranks items according to how recently they were published.
It relies on editors to select material for each audience.
It combines hundreds of signals in continuously retrained models.
questions.explanation: Collaborative filtering is defined as recommending to one user what similar users have chosen; the hundreds-of-signals approach describes modern systems instead.

questions.text: What side effect of optimising for engagement do critics identify?
choices: Users are shown less advertising than they expect.
Emotionally provocative material spreads further than accurate material.
Platforms become unable to predict what users will click.
Popular items are shown to fewer people over time.
questions.explanation: Critics argue that material provoking strong emotion, especially outrage, travels further, so engagement-based systems may favour the sensational.

questions.text: How does the writer summarise the research evidence on filter bubbles?
choices: The evidence conclusively disproves the existence of filter bubbles.
The evidence confirms that algorithms are the main driver of political division.
The effect is disputed and probably smaller than assumed, but not absent.
The evidence is too weak for any conclusion to be drawn at all.
questions.explanation: The writer calls the direction of the effect contested and its size probably smaller than commonly assumed, though not zero.

questions.text: The writer characterises recommendation systems as a form of mind control.
questions.explanation: False: the passage explicitly calls the technique unglamorous statistics rather than mind control.

questions.text: Most users consume relatively little political content online.
questions.explanation: True: this is given as one reason why users' news diets are more varied than the filter-bubble metaphor suggests.

questions.text: Chronological feeds have been shown to improve users' political knowledge.
questions.explanation: Not Given: chronological feeds are listed as a design remedy, but the passage reports no finding about their effect on knowledge.

questions.text: Regulators have obliged platforms of every size to disclose how their ranking systems work.
questions.explanation: False: the requirement described applies to platforms above a certain size.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Engagement is measured through proxies such as clicks, shares, comments and ______ time.
questions.explanation: Dwell time is listed among the engagement proxies in the second paragraph.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: One form of friction asks a user to open an ______ before sharing it.
questions.explanation: The passage gives prompting a user to open an article before sharing it as an example of design friction.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Some regulators require large platforms to give ______ researchers access to their data.
questions.explanation: The passage describes rules requiring disclosure of ranking systems and data access for vetted researchers.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Psychologists recommend habits such as ______ messages into fixed periods of the day.
questions.explanation: Batching messages into fixed periods is listed among the individual habits said to protect sustained attention.

questions.text: Complete the collocation with ONE WORD: The team ______ out extensive research into peatland restoration over five years.
questions.explanation: The standard academic collocation is to carry out research; 'do research' is possible but 'carry out' is the expected form here.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: From these figures it is difficult to ______ a firm conclusion.
questions.explanation: English collocates 'draw' with 'conclusion'; 'make a conclusion' is a common learner error.

questions.text: Choose the correct noun: Sphagnum moss plays a significant ______ in the formation of peat.
questions.explanation: 'Play a significant role in' is the fixed collocation; 'play a part' also exists but 'role' fits the academic register expected here.

questions.text: Choose the correct noun: Artificial light at night may ______ a serious threat to migrating birds.
questions.explanation: 'Pose a threat' is the standard collocation in academic writing.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: The proposal fails to ______ the criteria set out by the funding committee.
questions.explanation: Criteria, requirements, standards and deadlines are all 'met'; the other verbs do not collocate with 'criteria'.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Biologists are still trying to ______ up with a full explanation of magnetoreception.
questions.explanation: 'Come up with' means to produce or think of an idea or explanation; 'keep up with' means to stay level with something.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Funding for the restoration project was ______ back sharply after the review.
questions.explanation: 'Cut back' means to reduce; 'hold back' means to restrain and does not fit a budget reduction.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: The committee has agreed to ______ into the causes of the decline.
questions.explanation: 'Look into' means to investigate; the other verbs of seeing do not take 'into' with this meaning.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Efforts to cut emissions have been ______ up considerably over the past decade.
questions.explanation: 'Step up' means to increase the intensity of an activity; 'raise' and 'lift' are not used with 'up' in this sense.

questions.text: Complete with ONE WORD: The sales figures simply do not ______ up with the claims made in the annual report.
questions.explanation: 'Add up with' (or more commonly 'add up to') here means to be consistent with; if figures do not add up, they are not credible.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'The evidence remains inconclusive.'?
choices: The evidence proves the opposite of what was expected.
The evidence does not yet settle the question.
There is no evidence available on the subject.
The evidence has been rejected by most researchers.
questions.explanation: Inconclusive means the evidence exists but does not allow a firm decision, which is not the same as absent or rejected.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'Numbers of breeding pairs declined markedly.'?
choices: Breeding pairs fell sharply in number.
Breeding pairs remained more or less stable.
Breeding pairs were counted for the first time.
questions.explanation: 'Declined markedly' paraphrases as 'fell sharply'; markedly signals a large, noticeable change.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'The policy was implemented gradually.'?
choices: The policy was abandoned before it took effect.
The policy was introduced in stages over a period of time.
The policy came into force immediately.
The policy was applied only in certain regions.
questions.explanation: Gradual implementation means a phased introduction rather than an immediate or partial one.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'The findings are broadly consistent with earlier work.'?
choices: The findings contradict most previous research.
The findings largely agree with what earlier studies reported.
The findings repeat an earlier study exactly.
The findings cannot be compared with earlier studies.
questions.explanation: 'Broadly consistent with' signals general agreement, not exact repetition or contradiction.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'Researchers had underestimated the scale of the problem.'?
choices: The problem turned out to be larger than researchers had thought.
Researchers exaggerated the seriousness of the problem.
Researchers were unaware that the problem existed.
The problem proved easier to solve than expected.
questions.explanation: To underestimate a scale is to judge it as smaller than it really is, so the reality exceeds the earlier judgement.

questions.text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
choices: The number of applicants have risen steadily since 2019.
A number of applicants has risen steadily since 2019.
The number of applicants has risen steadily since 2019.
Number of applicants have risen steadily since 2019.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb, while 'a number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb.

questions.text: Complete the sentence: Not only ______ the scheme reduce costs, but it also improved safety.
questions.explanation: After a fronted negative expression such as 'not only', the subject and auxiliary invert, giving 'did the scheme reduce'.

questions.text: Complete the sentence: If the water table ______ raised to the surface, decomposition would slow almost at once.
questions.explanation: The second conditional pairs a past-form verb in the if-clause with 'would' in the main clause; 'were' is the standard form here.

questions.text: Choose the correct word form: There has been a steady ______ in the number of night-flying migrants recorded.
questions.explanation: After the article 'a' and an adjective a noun is required, so the noun 'increase' is correct.

questions.text: Complete the sentence: The results, ______ were published last year, have since been confirmed by two other teams.
questions.explanation: A non-defining relative clause set off by commas takes 'which', never 'that', and 'who' is used only for people.

questions.text: Complete the sentence: ______ the high cost of the equipment, the project was approved without delay.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase, whereas 'although' and 'whereas' introduce a full clause with a subject and verb.

questions.text: Complete with ONE WORD: The rise in emissions is largely due ______ the drainage of peatland.
questions.explanation: 'Due to' is a fixed prepositional phrase introducing a cause.

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate academic adjective: The study reported a ______ improvement in water quality after rewetting.
questions.explanation: 'Substantial' carries the right formality for academic writing, while 'big', 'huge' and 'great' are informal or imprecise here.

questions.text: Complete with ONE WORD: The authors ______ attention to the fact that peat fires can smoulder underground for months.
questions.explanation: 'Draw attention to' is the standard collocation; the past form 'drew' fits a report of what the authors did.

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate verb: The satellite data ______ a strong correlation between surface movement and water table depth.
questions.explanation: Data 'reveal' or 'show' a relationship; 'discover', 'notice' and 'find out' take a human subject in this context.

questions.text: According to the observational tradition described in the first paragraph, what decides whether a street is worth walking along?
choices: The width of the carriageway and the volume of traffic on it.
The proportion and materials of the upper storeys.
The band of building frontage between the pavement and the first floor.
The distance a pedestrian must walk to reach public transport.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph contrasts the architect's answer (proportion, materials, skyline) with the researchers' claim that quality is decided in the narrow band of frontage between the pavement and the first floor.

questions.text: How was the evidence described in the second paragraph obtained?
choices: By counting passers-by and recording their speed and stopping behaviour.
By interviewing residents about the routes they prefer.
By analysing the sales figures of ground-floor shops.
By modelling pedestrian flows in computer simulations.
questions.explanation: The passage says observers stand on a corner with a hand counter and record how many people pass, how quickly they move and how often they stop.

questions.text: Which factor is identified as the single strongest predictor of street life?
choices: The density of housing along the street.
The density of doorways along the frontage.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states explicitly that the density of doorways, rather than the density of housing, proved to be the strongest single predictor.

questions.text: Why, according to the writer, does a blank stretch of frontage make people walk faster?
choices: Blank frontage is normally found on streets with heavy traffic.
It offers too few visual events, so the distance feels longer than it is.
It provides no shelter from wind or rain.
It tends to be poorly lit after dark.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph argues the effect is one of attention: a hundred metres with one entrance supplies a single event, and blankness lengthens the perceived distance and encourages people to leave.

questions.text: What does the writer describe as the most serious objection to this line of research?
choices: The causal direction may be reversed, because shops open where people already are.
The counts were all carried out in a single country.
Pedestrians cannot reliably report what they have noticed.
Rules about frontage are impossible to enforce in practice.
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph calls this the most serious objection: the correlation between lively frontage and lively streets may record the cause rather than the effect.

questions.text: The newer planning codes described in the passage regulate what happens at ground level rather than prescribing an architectural style.
questions.explanation: True: the fourth paragraph says that rather than prescribing a style, the newer codes prescribe performance at ground level, such as unit width and numbers of entrances.

questions.text: In the comparison reported, roughly the same number of people paused beside blank walls as beside small shops.
questions.explanation: False: the passage states that beside a blank wall the number of people who paused fell almost tenfold.

questions.text: Streets with active frontage have been shown to have lower rates of crime.
questions.explanation: Not Given: the passage discusses walking speed, stopping and lingering, but says nothing at all about crime.

questions.text: Facade theatre, as the passage uses the term, means reducing the amount of glazing that regulations require.
questions.explanation: False: facade theatre is defined as installing the required glazing and then papering it over from the inside, not as reducing the requirement.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: The density of ______, rather than the density of housing, was the strongest predictor of street life.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names the density of doorways as the single strongest predictor, in contrast with the density of housing.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Newer codes set a maximum ______ for individual ground-floor units.
questions.explanation: The list of ground-level performance rules in the fourth paragraph begins with a maximum width for individual ground-floor units.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Codes may require a certain proportion of transparent ______ instead of mirrored or shuttered panels.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph lists a required proportion of transparent glazing rather than mirrored or shuttered panels.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Observers find that people occupy the ______ of a square before its centre.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph reports that people occupy the edges of a square before its centre, preferring a protected back and an open view.

questions.text: Why are hairline cracks a concern even though they are very narrow?
choices: They sharply reduce the compressive strength of the concrete.
They admit water and chlorides, which lead to corrosion of the reinforcement.
They make the surface of a structure difficult to clean.
They cause the cement to shrink further as it cures.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains that narrow cracks do little harm in themselves but open a path for water and chlorides, after which the steel corrodes and forces the concrete apart.

questions.text: What is autogenous healing?
choices: The addition of live bacteria to a standard concrete mix.
A repair method in which cracks are injected with resin.
The gradual corrosion of the steel inside the concrete.
The natural sealing of narrow cracks by cement grains that have not yet reacted.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes unreacted cement grains hydrating when moisture enters and depositing a crust, and calls this limited natural process autogenous healing.

questions.text: How does the biological approach seal a crack?
choices: Spores germinate when water and oxygen enter and precipitate calcium carbonate.
Bacteria dissolve the surrounding cement and reform it as a gel.
Bacteria swell to many times their original volume and block the gap.
Bacteria release a liquid adhesive stored inside their capsules.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says a crack admits water and oxygen, whereupon the spores germinate, consume the nutrient and precipitate calcium carbonate.

questions.text: What advantage do vascular systems have over microcapsule systems?
choices: They are easier to install inside a heavily reinforced beam.
They function without any water entering the crack.
The network can in principle be refilled from outside.
They add nothing to the cost of a conventional mix.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph notes that a vascular network can in principle be refilled from outside, whereas microcapsules release their contents once and cannot be replenished.

questions.text: Why does the writer treat testing standards as an obstacle to self-healing concrete?
choices: No laboratory is able to reproduce a realistic crack.
The bacteria cannot survive the conditions used during testing.
Field trials have grown too large to be monitored properly.
Standards fix properties at twenty-eight days and cannot credit a benefit that appears years later.
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says standards were written for materials whose properties are fixed at twenty-eight days, so a specification cannot easily reward a benefit that first appears in year fifteen.

questions.text: Bacterial concrete is measurably weaker than a conventional mix when it is new.
questions.explanation: True: the fifth paragraph states that the pellets carrying the spores are weaker than the aggregate they displace, so the concrete is measurably less strong when new.

questions.text: Autogenous healing will close a crack of any width if enough time is allowed.
questions.explanation: False: the passage says autogenous healing closes cracks up to roughly 0.2 millimetres and stops there.

questions.text: Self-healing concrete has been used in the construction of a major road bridge.
questions.explanation: Not Given: the field trials listed are an irrigation channel, a lock wall, tunnel lining and retaining walls; a bridge deck is mentioned only as a hypothetical calculation.

questions.text: According to the writer, the cheapest way to reduce the emissions of cement production is to make kilns more efficient.
questions.explanation: False: the final paragraph argues that the cheapest way to cut the figure is to build less, which means making structures last longer.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Cracks open a path for water and, near roads or coasts, for ______, which then reach the steel reinforcement.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph names water and, near roads or coasts, chlorides as the substances that reach and corrode the reinforcement.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: Bacterial ______ are packed into porous clay pellets and can stay dormant in the concrete for decades.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph describes spores of alkali-tolerant bacteria packed into porous clay pellets and remaining dormant in principle for decades.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: As they consume the nutrient, the bacteria precipitate calcium carbonate, in effect growing ______ across the gap.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph describes the precipitation of calcium carbonate as growing limestone across the crack.

questions.text: Complete the sentence with ONE WORD from the passage: In vascular systems, hollow ______ filled with an adhesive are cast into the structure and rupture when a crack forms.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph describes hollow tubes or channels filled with an adhesive that are cast into the structure and ruptured by a crack.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: The council intends to ______ a survey of pedestrian numbers next spring.
questions.explanation: A survey is conducted or carried out; 'make a survey' is a common learner error and 'perform' collocates with tasks and operations rather than surveys.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: These findings ______ serious doubt on the earlier estimate.
questions.explanation: The fixed collocation is 'cast doubt on something'; the other verbs are not used with 'doubt' in this pattern.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: The new code ______ strict limits on the length of blank frontage.
questions.explanation: Limits, restrictions and conditions are imposed (or placed) on something; 'make limits' and 'give limits' are not English collocations.

questions.text: Complete the collocation with ONE WORD: The proposal ______ rise to a lively debate among planners.
questions.explanation: 'Give rise to' means to cause or produce; the past form 'gave' fits a report of a past debate.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'Uptake of the technology has been patchy.'?
choices: The technology was adopted everywhere at the same time.
The technology has been rejected outright.
The technology has been adopted unevenly from place to place.
The technology is still confined to the laboratory.
questions.explanation: 'Patchy' means inconsistent or uneven, so some places have adopted the technology and others have not; it does not mean total rejection.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'The benefits are likely to outweigh the drawbacks.'?
choices: The benefits and the drawbacks are evenly balanced.
The drawbacks will probably prevent any benefit from appearing.
The benefits have already been fully demonstrated.
The advantages will probably be greater than the disadvantages.
questions.explanation: To outweigh something is to be greater or more important than it, and 'likely' keeps the claim tentative rather than proven.

questions.text: Which sentence is closest in meaning to: 'The correlation may run in the opposite direction.'?
choices: The two variables are certainly unrelated.
What was treated as the effect may in fact be the cause.
The measurements were taken from the wrong sample.
The relationship weakens as the sample size grows.
questions.explanation: This is the objection raised in the urban design passage: lively frontage may follow busy streets rather than create them, so cause and effect are reversed.

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate verb for academic writing: The available data ______ this interpretation.
questions.explanation: 'Support' is the neutral academic verb; 'back up' and 'prop up' are informal, and 'stand by' takes a human subject.

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate adverb: This relationship has been ______ researched over the past fifty years.
questions.explanation: 'Extensively' is the adverb expected in academic register; 'a lot' and 'really' are informal and 'very much' does not modify this participle naturally.

questions.text: Complete the sentence: ______ the number of empty units has risen, planners have begun to relax the retail requirement.
questions.explanation: Only 'because' can introduce a full clause with a subject and verb; 'despite', 'in spite of' and 'owing to' must be followed by a noun phrase.

questions.text: Complete the sentence: Rarely ______ such a clear relationship between design and behaviour been reported.
questions.explanation: A fronted negative adverb such as 'rarely' triggers inversion, and the singular subject 'a relationship' with the perfect passive requires 'has ... been reported'.

questions.text: Complete with ONE WORD: The new facade is twice ______ long as the one it replaced.
questions.explanation: Multiple comparisons use the pattern 'twice as + adjective + as', so the missing word is the first 'as'.
